edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SCIENCE & TECH + SPORT
edition.deck: A wave of school demonstrations in France leads the international news, alongside questions over a Russian laboratory death, a US president’s remarks about California and developments in Britain and Denmark.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential, developing news and groups multiple reports on the same events. The French protest coverage preserves differing crowd estimates and competing accounts of policing; the Russian case remains unconfirmed. Danish reports are translated and selected for their public impact.

content.headline: French school protests grow as police use tear gas and hundreds are injured
content.shortHeadline: French school protests grow as clashes injure hundreds
content.standfirst: Demonstrations over school conditions have spread nationwide, drawing pupils, teachers and parents. The government and unions give different estimates of turnout, while allegations of excessive police force are under investigation.

image.caption: A student raises a hand amid tear gas during a protest in Bordeaux.

sources.originalTitle: Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France
Riot police fire teargas as 250,000 take part in schools protests across France
‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing
How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?
Vold har præget flere demonstrationer: Alligevel går dansk lærer på gaden i Lyon for at støtte elever

segments.body: Hundreds of thousands joined demonstrations across France on Tuesday in a growing campaign for better school conditions. The interior ministry counted 256,000 people, including 56,000 in Paris; student unions put the total at 450,000. Police used tear gas and batons, though most marches were peaceful.

segments.title: Conditions and policing under scrutiny
segments.body: Students are calling for repairs to deteriorating buildings, smaller classes and more teachers. The education ministry says more than 900 high schools were blockaded or closed on Tuesday; student groups put the number at 1,800. Reports describe allegations of serious injuries from police weapons, and the authorities have opened internal investigations.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s account sets the protests against longstanding disparities: OECD figures show larger average classes in France than across the OECD, while analysts describe stark differences between advantaged and disadvantaged schools. The article also reports that around 10% of teaching hours are not delivered.

content.headline: Trump’s remarks about California cities draw fierce political backlash
content.shortHeadline: Trump’s California city remarks draw backlash
content.standfirst: After Donald Trump said Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego, California leaders condemned his words and said the state would monitor for threats. The White House said he was warning about a nuclear Iran.

image.caption: Donald Trump made the remarks about Los Angeles and San Diego at a campaign rally.

sources.originalTitle: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego

segments.body: At a campaign rally in Nebraska, Donald Trump said Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego. California Governor Gavin Newsom called the remarks “deranged and dangerous”; Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said they sounded like threats against residents. Newsom directed the state’s threat assessment centre to monitor the situation.

segments.title: White House rejects the criticism
segments.body: White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung said Trump was warning that US cities could be threatened if Iran had a nuclear weapon. The White House also criticised news coverage of the remarks. Trump had not responded to California leaders’ statements at the time of the report.

content.headline: Russia’s plague-lab worker death remains unexplained as officials face calls for
content.shortHeadline: Questions persist over Russian lab worker’s death
content.standfirst: Russia says a laboratory worker died of pneumonia of unknown cause, not plague, and says contacts have shown no symptoms. The World Health Organization and experts are seeking clarity as reports about possible exposure remain unverified.

image.caption: The anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk where Darya Shipilova worked.

sources.originalTitle: Rubio urges Russia to share more information on plague lab worker's death
What do we know about death of anti-plague institute worker in Russia and is there a wider risk?
Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague. This is what you should know
Seruminstitut ser ingen grund til pest-bekymring i Danmark
What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?

segments.body: Darya Shipilova, 28, who worked at a plague research institute in Irkutsk, died after becoming ill. Russian health authorities say she died of “pneumonia of an undetermined etiology” and that contacts have been identified and monitored, with none showing symptoms. They told the World Health Organization no plague case had been recorded in Irkutsk.

segments.title: Exposure and wider risk are unclear
segments.body: Reports have suggested Shipilova may have been exposed after breaking a test tube or during a trip, but Russian authorities have denied a laboratory accident and the cause of her illness remains unconfirmed. Experts say pneumonic plague can spread between people in close contact and is treatable with antibiotics if treated early. The WHO assessed the risk as moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for Russia and very low for its European region.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s expert interviews stress that the available information is not enough to distinguish an isolated occupational exposure from another cause. Researchers say transparency about what happened matters beyond Russia.

content.headline: Yemeni children risk sniper fire to attend school near Taiz front line
content.shortHeadline: Yemeni children risk sniper fire to reach school
content.standfirst: In Taiz, children attend a school close to opposing forces’ positions as fighting intensifies. A mortar strike killed a three-year-old and critically injured another child, while families fear the city could be encircled.

image.caption: Yemeni schoolgirls describe the risks of attending school near the front line.

sources.originalTitle: Children brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line

segments.body: Rafeef, 10, walks uphill to school in Taiz with her back towards Houthi sniper positions. Her school stands beside a contested valley, with government-held territory on one side and Houthi positions on the other. She says she is afraid but wants to keep learning and seeing her friends.

segments.title: Civilians caught in renewed fighting
segments.body: The BBC reports that a mortar strike at a mechanic’s shop killed three-year-old Ahmed and left 11-year-old Amjad critically ill. Residents also fear the Houthis could seize Taiz after a key supply route was cut; control of the route has shifted before. The report says government forces have made gains elsewhere, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

content.headline: Paramount completes $110bn Warner Bros takeover, reshaping Hollywood and media
content.shortHeadline: Paramount completes $110bn Warner Bros takeover
content.standfirst: The deal brings major studios, streaming services and newsrooms under one company. Its debt, promised film output and safeguards for CNN and CBS are likely to shape what audiences watch and how the networks operate.

image.caption: Paramount and Warner Bros are joining to form Skydance Corporation.

sources.originalTitle: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you

segments.body: Paramount Skydance has completed its $110bn takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, creating a company to be branded Skydance Corporation. The combined portfolio includes HBO, CBS, CNN, Nickelodeon and major film franchises. The merger follows a bidding contest and legal challenges from US states concerned about competition.

segments.title: Costs, films and newsroom safeguards
segments.body: The company carries about $80bn in debt and executives are targeting $6bn in annual savings. A settlement with US states requires at least 30 films a year for the first two years, followed by 32 annually for three years, and establishes a news editorial independence board for CNN and CBS. Critics and workers cited in the reporting question whether those measures can prevent job losses or protect editorial independence.

perspectives.body: The consumer and workforce consequences remain uncertain: analysts expect streaming prices could rise, and a report cited by the BBC estimates the merger could eliminate about 4,500 direct film and TV jobs in Los Angeles County. The settlement does not prevent layoffs.

content.headline: Former German intelligence chief arrested on espionage and treason suspicions
content.shortHeadline: Former German spy chief arrested on espionage suspicions
content.standfirst: Prosecutors accuse August Hanning of using classified information for foreign intelligence services and say a former colleague passed him about 2,000 documents. The alleged foreign powers and whether information reached an intended recipient have not been disclosed.

image.caption: August Hanning, who led Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service from 1998 to 2005.

sources.originalTitle: Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason

segments.body: August Hanning, who led Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service from 1998 to 2005, has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, prosecutors say. A former BND employee, identified as Manfred D, was also arrested and is accused of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for payment.

Prosecutors allege Hanning used intelligence to draft an analysis for a foreign service and passed political information to a representative of another service. They have not named the countries and say it is unclear whether the analysis reached its intended recipient. Hanning is also connected by investigators to a separate case, allegations he denies.

content.headline: Cornell faces scrutiny over response to student’s alleged gang rape
content.shortHeadline: Cornell faces scrutiny over response to rape allegations
content.standfirst: A student identified as Jane Doe alleges she was drugged and raped by seven men and says Cornell failed to protect her. The university disputes her account of its response and has commissioned an independent review as scrutiny intensifies.

image.caption: Cornell students demonstrate in support of Jane Doe and call for accountability.

sources.originalTitle: Lawyer for one of Cornell 7 calls for special prosecutor to be removed over previous comments
Protester efter voldtægtsanklager på Cornell: 'Vi er Jane Doe'
Advokat: Kvinde i Cornell-sag bliver truet til at droppe sit søgsmål

segments.body: Jane Doe’s lawsuit accuses seven men of raping her at a Cornell fraternity party in 2024 and the university of failing to protect her. Cornell disputes the allegations about its response, saying two accused students were expelled, two suspended, one had graduated and two were found not responsible. Students and staff have protested on campus.

segments.title: Questions over the investigation
segments.body: New York Attorney General Letitia James, appointed special prosecutor, faces a request from a defence lawyer to recuse herself because she publicly expressed support for the alleged victim. James is investigating the case and the initial responses by Cornell and law enforcement. The university has hired former deputy attorney general Sally Yates to lead an independent review; Doe’s lawyer has also reported threats against his client, without identifying who made them.

perspectives.body: The lawyer seeking James’s recusal says her earlier comments could create an avoidable question about the investigation’s independence, while acknowledging he is not alleging corruption or that a court has found her legally disqualified.

content.headline: IceCube neutrino observatory work earns Francis Halzen the physics Nobel
content.shortHeadline: IceCube pioneer Francis Halzen wins physics Nobel
content.standfirst: The Nobel recognises Halzen’s leadership in developing a detector embedded in Antarctic ice. Its neutrinos offer scientists a way to investigate violent cosmic events that ordinary telescopes cannot readily observe.

image.caption: Francis Halzen, recognised for his work developing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.

sources.originalTitle: 'Ghost particles' from space telescope wins physics Nobel

segments.body: Belgian-born physicist Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work developing IceCube, a neutrino observatory at the South Pole. Thousands of light sensors embedded in a cubic kilometre of ice detect rare flashes produced when high-energy neutrinos interact with matter.

segments.title: A new window on the universe
segments.body: Neutrinos can pass through dense matter without being deflected by magnetic fields, so their direction and energy can provide clues to distant events such as exploding stars and the environments around giant black holes. Halzen said he was surprised his idea worked; the Nobel committee credited his scientific vision and leadership.

content.headline: New arrest in investigation of incident near RAF Fairford; no charges yet
content.shortHeadline: Seventh arrest in RAF Fairford investigation
content.standfirst: A 22-year-old British man has been arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, the seventh arrest connected to suspicious vehicles near the Gloucestershire base. No one has been charged, and the US has not confirmed reports about a specific threat.

sources.originalTitle: British national arrested in connection with RAF Fairford incident

segments.body: Counter-terrorism police arrested a 22-year-old British national in Westminster on Tuesday in connection with an incident near RAF Fairford on 27 September. It is the seventh arrest in the investigation; no one has been charged. A major incident was declared after three suspicious vehicles were reported and nearby homes were evacuated.

segments.title: Questions over US bomber withdrawal
segments.body: The US pulled its bombers from Fairford and President Donald Trump said there had been “some threats”. US media reports suggested intelligence pointed to a possible Iranian drone attack, but the BBC said it had not verified them. US European Command declined to discuss intelligence and said it would continue assessing the threat at its bases.

content.headline: Badenoch rejects Reform deal and proposes lower hiring tax for young workers
content.shortHeadline: Badenoch rules out Reform deal and proposes youth tax cut
content.standfirst: The Conservative leader says she would prefer another election to governing with Reform if no party wins a majority. She also proposes halving employer National Insurance for workers aged 21 to 24, saying the change would help young people into work.

image.caption: Kemi Badenoch speaks during a BBC interview at the Conservative Party conference.

sources.originalTitle: I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK, says Badenoch

segments.body: Kemi Badenoch said she would rather hold another general election than form a government with Reform UK after a hung parliament. She called Reform “neck deep in scandal”; Nigel Farage’s party has not yet responded in the supplied reporting. Polling cited by the BBC suggests no party is currently on course for a majority.

segments.title: Proposal for younger workers
segments.body: Badenoch also proposed cutting the employer National Insurance rate on earnings for 21- to 24-year-olds from 15% to 7.5%. The Conservatives say the standard rate would apply above £50,270. Labour called the proposal “fantasy economics”; Badenoch said the party would first need to find the money.

content.headline: Reform MP bought Welsh second home days after raising housing concerns
content.shortHeadline: Reform MP bought second home after raising housing concerns
content.standfirst: Sarah Pochin bought an £800,000 property on Anglesey two days after asking the government about second homes’ impact on rural housing. The island applies a 100% council-tax premium to second homes; Pochin and her husband have not responded to the report’s request for comment.

image.caption: Sarah Pochin, Reform UK MP for Runcorn and Helsby.

sources.originalTitle: Reform MP raises concerns about second homes – then buys one for £800,000

segments.body: Sarah Pochin, Reform MP for Runcorn and Helsby, bought a Grade II-listed home on Anglesey jointly with her husband. The Guardian reports the purchase was completed two days after she asked the housing minister what assessment had been made of the effect of second homes on housing availability in coastal and rural communities.

segments.title: Pressure on local housing
segments.body: Anglesey recorded 2,635 furnished homes that were not their owners’ main residence in March 2026 and has a 100% council-tax premium on second homes. Local officials say high concentrations can reduce homes available to residents and affect services. Pochin and her husband have also submitted plans to alter the property; Reform did not respond to a request for comment.

content.headline: Court hears alleged Iranian spies planned serious violence against UK targets
content.shortHeadline: Alleged Iranian spies accused of planning violence in UK
content.standfirst: Prosecutors say three men surveilled journalists at Iran International and another target as part of a plan to commit serious violence. The defendants deny the charges; the trial is continuing.

image.caption: The three defendants appear by video link at the Old Bailey.

sources.originalTitle: Alleged Iranian spies planned ‘serious violence’ against UK journalists, court hears

segments.body: Three men are charged under the National Security Act with conduct allegedly intended to assist a foreign intelligence service. Prosecutors say their surveillance targets included two journalists at London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International and a founder of UK Lawyers for Israel. The men deny the charges.

segments.title: Evidence and competing accounts
segments.body: The prosecution says the defendants photographed and filmed addresses linked to targets and used online tools to research them. It alleges Mostafa Sepahvand intended to carry out a violent attack. He says he was threatened into conducting surveillance; the prosecution calls that account false. The other two defendants say they did not know the purpose of the surveillance.

content.headline: Staff shortages threaten specialist support promised for pupils with SEND
content.shortHeadline: Staff shortages put SEND support plan at risk
content.standfirst: The £1.8bn Experts at Hand programme aims to bring specialists into mainstream schools, but at least 36 councils have warned about staffing capacity. Ministers say delivery is phased over three years and has only just begun.

image.caption: Schools minister Georgia Gould announced the Experts at Hand scheme at Labour conference.

sources.originalTitle: SEND pupils’ extra support at risk with schools unable to access specialist staff

segments.body: The government’s Experts at Hand scheme is intended to increase schools’ access to educational psychologists, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and specialist teachers. But analysis by Schools Week found at least 36 councils had raised concerns about recruiting or retaining the staff needed to deliver it.

segments.title: Capacity is the central concern
segments.body: A think-tank report cited in the reporting estimated that England needed another 1,400 full-time equivalent educational psychologists. Unions and school leaders warn that shortages could leave children without support and increase pressure on school staff. The Department for Education says the £1.8bn programme is being rolled out over three years and that it is investing in workforce capacity.

content.headline: Nurseries to face tighter phone and photo rules under safeguarding guidance
content.shortHeadline: Nurseries to face tighter phone and photo rules
content.standfirst: Planned guidance would restrict personal devices in childcare areas, limit routine photos and require checks on work devices. Ministers say the changes aim to strengthen safeguarding after abuse and data-security cases.

image.caption: Government guidance would introduce new device and photography rules for nursery staff.

sources.originalTitle: Nursery staff to be banned from using phones after ‘chilling’ child abuse case

segments.body: Government guidance expected this month would tell nursery staff, childminders and visitors not to use personal phones and digital devices in childcare areas. Staff would use a designated work device and generally take no more than one photo of each child a day; images would require written parental permission and rules for storage and deletion.

segments.title: Safeguarding and implementation
segments.body: The proposed measures follow the abuse of children by a nursery worker and a cyberattack targeting a nursery chain. Guidance is also expected to call for monthly checks of work devices and caution against uploading identifiable children’s images to AI tools. A nursery workers’ union says staff shortages and limited training could make safeguards harder to apply consistently.

content.headline: Avanti nationalisation will not quickly fix delays or cut fares, experts warn
content.shortHeadline: Avanti nationalisation will not quickly fix delays
content.standfirst: The operator has Britain’s worst record for trains arriving on time, but experts say the crowded West Coast Main Line is a major cause and state ownership is no quick fix. Infrastructure work is planned through 2029; cheaper fares are not promised.

image.caption: Avanti West Coast recorded Britain’s worst on-time performance in 2025–26.

sources.originalTitle: The UK’s worst rail firm is being nationalised. But don’t expect improvements soon

segments.body: Avanti West Coast is due to return to public ownership in March after recording the lowest share of on-time trains among operators in 2025–26: 37.9%. The Office of Rail and Road attributed 66% of its delayed minutes to Network Rail issues, including problems on the congested West Coast Main Line.

segments.title: Infrastructure, not ownership alone
segments.body: Rail specialists say bottlenecks and limited capacity will remain after nationalisation. A £400m Network Rail programme of signalling, track and overhead-line work is due to finish by March 2029, but experts describe much of it as maintenance rather than a major capacity expansion. The government has not committed to lower fares.

content.headline: Tories propose £10bn missile shield, far below previous £80bn estimates
content.shortHeadline: Tory £10bn missile shield plan faces £80bn cost estimate
content.standfirst: The Conservatives say a “Britannia Shield” would protect bases and critical infrastructure, funded through higher defence spending. The proposed £10bn cost is far below previous estimates of at least £80bn for an entry-level system.

image.caption: A Royal Navy Type 45 destroyer, equipped with a missile-interception system.

sources.originalTitle: Badenoch promises ‘Britannia shield’ iron dome missile system to protect UK

segments.body: The Conservatives propose spending £10bn over ten years on an integrated missile and drone defence network, with a basic system in place during their first term in office. They say it would link radar, command systems and interceptors to protect military bases, power stations and other critical infrastructure.

segments.title: Cost and capability questioned
segments.body: Previous estimates cited in the reporting put an entry-level system at about £80bn over ten years; the government’s current investment plan allocates £790m for integrated air and missile defence. The Conservatives say their proposal would be funded by raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. Labour says it is investing £1bn in air defences.

content.headline: Danish pharmacies add identity checks after CPR data breach exposed millions
content.shortHeadline: Pharmacies add ID checks after CPR data breach
content.standfirst: Pharmacies may ask customers for identification or extra questions before handing out medicines, particularly those with misuse risks. Authorities say CPR numbers can no longer be relied on by themselves to verify identity.

image.caption: Pharmacies may ask for identification or additional checks before handing out medicine.

sources.originalTitle: Apoteker skærper opmærksomheden ved medicinudlevering efter CPR-læk
Kan jeg stole på det, jeg får i min e-Boks? Her er de spørgsmål, danskerne vil have svar på efter cpr-lækket

segments.body: Danish pharmacies are tightening checks on medicine and health-information collection after a breach exposed data from 8.8 million living, deceased and emigrated people in the CPR register. A CPR number alone will no longer normally be enough to collect medicine; customers may be asked for health-card identification or verification questions.

segments.title: What the exposed data can—and cannot—do
segments.body: A CPR number and other personal details can help scammers impersonate someone, but the experts cited by DR say the number alone cannot be used to take out a loan or open a credit card; loans require MitID approval. The breach itself does not give outsiders access to send messages through e-Boks, although compromised organisations’ systems could pose a separate risk. The incident is under investigation.

perspectives.body: Security expert Sofie Freja Christensen says the central weakness is not the CPR number itself but its use as proof of identity. She says the leak points to a need to monitor how authorised users access sensitive registers.

content.headline: Denmark’s 2035 gas-heating goal stalls as 60 municipalities pause projects
content.shortHeadline: Denmark’s 2035 gas-heating goal faces delays
content.standfirst: A quarter of a million homes still use gas, while a report says 60 municipalities expect to approve no new district-heating projects this year. Residents cite conversion costs, and local officials want more support to keep the transition on track.

image.caption: A quarter of a million Danish homes still use gas heating.

sources.originalTitle: Regeringens 2035-mål er ikke nok: Oppositionspartier efterlyser hård slutdato for naturgas
Danskernes farvel til gasfyr gået i stå flere steder

segments.body: Denmark’s goal is to end gas heating in homes by 2035, but 60 municipalities expect to process or approve no new district-heating projects this year, according to Local Government Denmark. About 250,000 homes still use gas. In Holbæk, a project was postponed after only just over one in ten residents backed joining the scheme.

segments.title: Cost and local consent
segments.body: Residents in a Holbæk housing association voted against the project over concerns about the roughly 30 million kroner investment and whether households could afford the bill. Local officials say more financial support is needed; an energy-planning professor says previous costly projects have damaged public trust. The government has proposed an extra 200 million kroner for district-heating expansion and says ending oil and gas heating remains its ambition.

perspectives.body: Local Government Denmark says the current framework is insufficient to meet the 2035 goal and calls for clearer commitment and more support where conversion would be expensive for residents.

content.headline: Danish researchers begin trial of psilocybin-assisted therapy for anorexia
content.shortHeadline: Danish trial tests psilocybin-assisted anorexia therapy
content.standfirst: A research project in Region Zealand will study psilocybin alongside therapy for 62 women whose anorexia has not responded to earlier treatment. The study is testing a treatment, not reporting proven benefit.

image.caption: Puk Hoppe Søe says she considers herself recovered after years of anorexia.

sources.originalTitle: Puk blev straffet, når hun ikke spiste – nu håber hun på bedre behandling
Svampestof skal testes mod ‘den mest dødelige psykiatriske lidelse’

segments.body: Researchers in Region Zealand have begun a study of psilocybin-assisted therapy for anorexia. Sixty-two women over 18 who have previously received treatment without sufficient benefit are to take part. Participants will receive therapeutic sessions before, during and after taking the psychedelic substance.

segments.title: An experimental approach
segments.body: The researchers hope the experience may help participants think differently about restrictive rules and patterns associated with anorexia, but whether it will help is the question the trial is designed to test. Puk Hoppe Søe, who describes her long recovery from the illness, says she sees a need for alternative approaches. Her experience is not evidence of the trial’s outcome.

perspectives.body: Hoppe Søe describes earlier treatment as focused on weight gain and food, with privileges withdrawn when patients did not eat. She says small insights helped her recovery, but also recounts relapses and stresses how difficult recovery can be.

content.headline: Too few freight trains linked to cracks and speed limits on Danish high-speed
content.shortHeadline: Too few freight trains linked to Danish track cracks
content.standfirst: Banedanmark says freight traffic was expected to help keep tracks even, but many freight locomotives cannot use the line’s new signalling system. Passenger trains have faced speed restrictions; the first compatible freight trains are expected next year.

image.caption: Cracks in the rails have led trains to slow down on the high-speed line.

sources.originalTitle: Banedanmark: Fraværet af godstog giver problemer på højhastighedsbane

segments.body: Banedanmark says too few freight trains on the high-speed line between Ringsted, Køge Nord and Copenhagen have contributed to track irregularities and cracks, forcing passenger trains to slow down. The railway authority says the line was designed on the assumption that freight operators would adopt the new signalling equipment.

The signalling system entered service in spring 2023, but many freight trains are not equipped to use it. Banedanmark expects the first compatible freight services to run on the route next year and says it regrets the disruption to passengers.

content.headline: Danish MP films colleagues with Meta smart glasses, prompting privacy backlash
content.shortHeadline: Meta smart glasses spark privacy row at Danish parliament
content.standfirst: Lars Boje Mathiesen says filming colleagues with the glasses is intended to make politicians consider surveillance. Other MPs call it inappropriate, while a government lawmaker says officials are examining how to protect people from unwanted recording.

image.caption: Lars Boje Mathiesen wears the smart glasses he used to film at parliament.

sources.originalTitle: Lars Boje filmer sine kollegaer med kontroversiel brille: 'Klamt', siger ordfører

segments.body: Lars Boje Mathiesen, leader of Borgernes Parti, wore Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses while filming an interview at the Danish parliament. He argues politicians should experience the surveillance they permit elsewhere. Several colleagues criticised the move as poor workplace conduct and said they had not agreed to be filmed.

Social Democratic lawmaker Lea Wermelin said monitoring to investigate crime is not comparable to filming colleagues at work and said the government is looking at approaches in other European countries. Mathiesen said whether he seeks consent depends on the situation and that he does not want to film people secretly.

content.headline: MobilePay to become Vipps as Nordic payment app adopts shared name
content.shortHeadline: MobilePay to be renamed Vipps in Denmark
content.standfirst: The Danish app will take the name and logo used by the Nordic mobile-wallet group from 12 January. The company says users will not need to do anything and the service will otherwise remain unchanged.

image.caption: The MobilePay app icon is changing ahead of its renaming to Vipps.

sources.originalTitle: MobilePay skifter navn

segments.body: MobilePay will be renamed Vipps in Denmark on 12 January, aligning the app’s name and logo across Denmark, Finland, Sweden and Norway. The company says the app will continue to work as before and users need take no action. MobilePay handles more than half a billion transactions a year in Denmark.

content.headline: Danish cinemas asked not to screen Gaza documentary on 7 October anniversary
content.shortHeadline: Cinemas asked to avoid Gaza film on 7 October anniversary
content.standfirst: The distributor says the request came from the directors of Naza. The film uses anonymous testimony to allege systematic killings of Palestinian civilians by the Israeli military, which has categorically rejected the accusation.

image.caption: Naza directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, who asked cinemas not to screen the film on 7 October.

sources.originalTitle: Biografer bedt om at droppe hypet film om Gaza-krigen

segments.body: Danish cinemas have been asked not to screen the documentary Naza on 7 October, the anniversary of Hamas’s attack on Israel. Distributor Angel Films says the request came from directors Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham. Aarhus cinema Øst for Paradis cancelled that day’s showing and told ticket-holders.

The film, which premiered in Denmark the previous week, draws on anonymous testimony from people in the Israeli military and intelligence services and alleges systematic mass killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. The Israeli military has categorically rejected the accusation; the report also notes criticism of the film’s anonymous sources.

content.headline: African music is more than Afrobeats: why the label can limit it
content.shortHeadline: African music is more than Afrobeats
content.standfirst: Artists and writers argue that using Afrobeats as a catch-all flattens a continent’s varied sounds. The label has helped music travel, but can obscure local scenes and leave emerging styles poorly documented.

image.caption: Tyla at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards in Los Angeles.

sources.originalTitle: The west has a blinkered view of African music – and it’s hurting the whole continent’s culture

segments.body: Tyla has objected to being grouped under Afrobeats, saying she represents South African amapiano. The Guardian traces how a label that helped market contemporary West African dance music came to stand in for a much broader range of African pop.

segments.title: What the label leaves out
segments.body: Artists including Tems and Burna Boy have also described their music in terms other than Afrobeats. The article argues that the umbrella can blur distinctions between traditions and leave newer styles—such as banku music, azonto and mara—without the documentation and local context needed to develop distinct identities.

content.headline: George Fenton, composer of scores for more than 100 films, dies aged 76
content.shortHeadline: Composer George Fenton dies aged 76
content.standfirst: The five-time Oscar nominee wrote music for Gandhi, Groundhog Day and many Ken Loach films, as well as landmark nature documentaries and BBC news programmes. His family said his death was unexpected; no cause was given.

image.caption: George Fenton in 2001.

sources.originalTitle: George Fenton, Oscar-nominated British composer for more than 100 films, dies aged 76

segments.body: George Fenton, the British composer whose work ranged across more than 100 feature films, television, theatre and documentary, has died aged 76. His family described his death as unexpected but did not give a cause.

segments.title: A career across screen and stage
segments.body: Fenton earned five Oscar nominations, beginning with Gandhi and Cry Freedom. His enduring collaborations included 18 Ken Loach films and repeated work with directors Stephen Frears and Richard Attenborough. He also composed for The Blue Planet, Planet Earth and Frozen Planet, and wrote themes for BBC news programmes including Newsnight.

content.headline: Liz Harris finds a restorative kind of togetherness with dream-pop trio Helen
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris finds a new side of herself with Helen
content.standfirst: The Grouper musician reflects on collaboration, a viral track fraudulently uploaded by someone else, and the DIY instincts that keep her wary of the music industry. Reforming Helen, she says, has brought a welcome sense of community.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris has built Grouper around solitary, atmospheric songs. In Helen, the dream-pop trio she formed with Jed Bindeman and Scott Simmons, she finds a different register: “I get to relax more in Helen,” she says, describing its collaborative process as restorative during a period of medical difficulties.

segments.title: The costs of sudden attention
segments.body: When Grouper’s “Poison Tree” gained an unexpected audience on TikTok, Harris discovered that someone else had fraudulently registered and uploaded the song, earning around six figures. She and her label were able to recover what she was owed, but she says fake uploads and remixes leave independent artists spending energy policing streaming platforms.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album turns protest into a family affair
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello puts protest at the heart of his solo album
content.standfirst: On Everyone Gets What They Want, the Rage Against the Machine guitarist makes an explicit case for anti-racist and anti-fascist music. He also credits his late mother’s activism with shaping his belief that ordinary people can change the world.

image.caption: Tom Morello.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as his first full-length solo rock album with him at the microphone. He calls it a “State of the Union address”: a collection of anti-racist and anti-fascist songs, featuring guests including Serj Tankian and Kneecap, and his 15-year-old son Roman.

segments.title: The example of Mary Morello
segments.body: Morello says his mother, Mary, who died in June aged 102, taught him to act on behalf of others. He recalls her explaining the United Farm Workers grape boycott when he was six: “We have to help them because we can.” He has established a memorial project encouraging people to donate, volunteer and protest causes she supported.

content.headline: Tate Britain’s 90s exhibition revisits a decade of art, fashion and nightlife
content.shortHeadline: Inside the 90s: art, fashion and nightlife
content.standfirst: A selection of photographs and works from Tate Britain’s new exhibition evokes the decade’s overlapping scenes, from jungle at the Blue Note to club nights and fashion. Curator Edward Enninful says the period also changed who got to participate in culture.

sources.originalTitle: 'Rock 'n' roll swagger': 10 iconic images capturing the chaotic energy of '90s Brit culture

segments.body: The BBC looks at images featured in Tate Britain’s The 90s: Art & Fashion, including Corinne Day’s documentary-style photography, an Alexander McQueen runway show and Eddie Otchere’s portrait of Goldie’s Metalheadz night. Together they suggest a decade in which music, fashion, art and club culture repeatedly crossed paths.

segments.title: More than a style revival
segments.body: Curator Edward Enninful argues that the period was about more than its recognisable looks: he points to a wider shift in who could take part in culture and whose voices were heard. The article also revisits club photography, after-hours street scenes and the DIY energy that artists remember as distinctive to the time.

content.headline: Greg Freeman’s All Set the Bone turns small-town unease into restless rock
content.shortHeadline: Greg Freeman makes unease feel electric on All Set the Bone
content.standfirst: The Vermont songwriter’s new album pairs anxious, vividly detailed lyrics with compositions that veer through chord changes and sudden shifts. Pitchfork hears a darker, more menacing record than its predecessor.

sources.originalTitle: All Set the Bone

segments.body: Pitchfork describes Greg Freeman’s singing as deliberately unsteady: his voice cracks and slips across songs populated by angry, isolated people and struggling towns. The lyrics move quickly from sharply observed details to memorable turns of phrase, giving the album a nervous, unsettled point of view.

segments.title: Songs that threaten to come apart
segments.body: The music keeps pace with that instability. Built around guitars, piano and organ, the songs stretch beyond bar-rock convention through shifting tempos, chord changes and dynamic turns. With John Congleton producing, the record sounds darker than Freeman’s breakout Burnover, its heavier distortion adding to the sense of something barely held together.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul reissue reveals an album still in motion
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul remains a work in motion
content.standfirst: A deluxe edition gathers alternate mixes, outtakes and the US album alongside the original UK release. Pitchfork argues that the set makes the landmark record feel less like a fixed monument and more like a work shaped by choices and circumstance.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: Rubber Soul sits at a turning point in the Beatles’ history and in pop, as the band moved beyond songs as a string of hits toward an album conceived as a work in its own right. The new set’s recording notes also reveal how quickly the group worked under pressure to deliver a record by Christmas 1965.

segments.title: There is no single definitive version
segments.body: The collection includes the UK and US tracklists, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a new mix. Their differences invite comparisons without settling on one “real” Rubber Soul: the review finds pleasure in hearing how arrangements took shape, while noting that listeners’ preferences depend partly on which version they grew up with.

content.headline: Lambchop strip back their sound on the strange, intimate Punching the Clown
content.shortHeadline: Lambchop find new intimacy on Punching the Clown
content.standfirst: Kurt Wagner’s storytelling stays expansive as the band pares back its arrangements to acoustic guitar, banjo and choir. Pitchfork finds the result both disquieting and emotionally direct, with room for Wagner’s humour and tangents.

sources.originalTitle: Punching the Clown

segments.body: Lambchop have moved through many musical forms over four decades, but Kurt Wagner’s uncontainable writing remains a constant. On Punching the Clown, acoustic guitar, banjo and choral harmonies leave space for his generation-spanning stories, abrupt jokes and oddly precise observations.

segments.title: Plain arrangements, difficult feelings
segments.body: The stripped-back sound gives songs about illness, death and unfinished business an intimate, uneasy quality. The review hears a contrast between Wagner’s humour and the bleakness of the material, and argues that the album’s restraint helps it feel more emotionally direct rather than less ambitious.

content.headline: Artificial turns Sam Altman and OpenAI into a blunt, muddled satire
content.shortHeadline: Artificial’s OpenAI satire is sharp but muddled
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s film casts Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman in a comic account of OpenAI’s rise. The Guardian finds flashes of savage humour and chilling ideas, but says the film’s broad jokes and visual metaphors weaken its argument.

image.caption: Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.

sources.originalTitle: Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire

segments.body: Artificial follows Ilya Sutskever’s work with Geoff Hinton and his partnership with Sam Altman as OpenAI develops. Andrew Garfield gives Altman a calculated, self-pitying edge, while the film frames the company’s ambitions as a clash between Sutskever’s optimism and Altman’s self-interest.

segments.title: A satire that overstates its case
segments.body: The review sees moments of sharp comedy and genuine unease, but argues that the script’s broad humour and heavy-handed imagery leave little room to understand the people or the culture that enabled them. Its verdict: Artificial can point to dystopian risks, but its tonal jumble makes those warnings less persuasive.

content.headline: Twelve films to look out for at the 2026 London film festival
content.shortHeadline: Twelve films to look out for at the London film festival
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s selection ranges from Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson to a new Mike Leigh drama, a vampire in Vienna and a film about a Manchester teenager discovering its music scene.

sources.originalTitle: Hamlet’s goodbye, the last of Leigh, Birmingham blues and a vampire in Vienna: 12 great films at the London film festival

segments.body: The selection spans historical drama, contemporary social realism, comedy, science fiction and horror. Among the films highlighted are a portrait of Ian Charleson starring Andrew Scott, Carol Morley’s story of a teenager drawn into Manchester’s music scene, and Clio Barnard’s drama about young adults in Birmingham.

segments.title: A varied festival slate
segments.body: Other recommendations include a new film from Mike Leigh, an Andrew Haigh adaptation of a story by Colm Tóibín, and Isabelle Huppert as a vampire in present-day Vienna. The guide presents these as notable choices from the festival, rather than a claim that they share a single style or subject.

content.headline: Sergiu Celibidache’s son remembers the conductor behind The Yellow Tie
content.shortHeadline: A son remembers conductor Sergiu Celibidache
content.standfirst: In a personal essay tied to a new film he co-wrote, Serge Ioan Celebidachi recalls a loving but demanding father who rejected commercial recordings. He also explains why he secretly preserved recordings of his father’s performances.

image.caption: Sergiu Celibidache conducting in the early 1980s.

sources.originalTitle: Celibidache was a musical visionary, an uncompromising perfectionist – and my father

segments.body: Serge Ioan Celebidachi remembers his father, the conductor Sergiu Celibidache, as both generous and exacting. The musician expected full attention in everyday life as well as in music, and his son describes the pressure of those standards alongside the warmth of their relationship.

segments.title: The recordings he kept
segments.body: Celibidache believed that recordings could not reproduce the experience of live music and refused lucrative offers to make them. His son secretly allowed some orchestras to record later performances, believing those documents had value. That disagreement, he says, helped give him the distance to approach his father’s life without putting him on a pedestal.

content.headline: The Lost Children of Tuam is a devastating account of Ireland’s tragedy
content.shortHeadline: The Lost Children of Tuam refuses easy closure
content.standfirst: Monica Dolan plays historian Catherine Corless, whose research uncovered the fate of children at a mother and baby home in County Galway. The review praises the film’s restraint and its refusal to offer comforting resolution.

image.caption: Monica Dolan as historian Catherine Corless in The Lost Children of Tuam.

sources.originalTitle: The Lost Children of Tuam review – deeply serious retelling of Ireland’s devastating tragedy

segments.body: The film follows Catherine Corless as she investigates deaths at St Mary’s mother and baby home in Tuam. She finds nearly 800 death certificates but no burial records. The Guardian describes the drama as careful not to embellish or fictionalise the discoveries at the heart of the story.

segments.title: No simple ending
segments.body: Monica Dolan’s performance as Corless anchors the film, while brief appearances by survivors leave a lasting impression. The review stresses that the story offers neither a satisfying sense of closure nor an uplifting finish: its force lies in taking the people affected and the scale of the harm seriously.

content.headline: Club Kid is a warm, funny love letter to queer nightlife
content.shortHeadline: Club Kid finds heart in queer nightlife
content.standfirst: Jordan Firstman’s directorial debut follows a New York club promoter who discovers he has a 10-year-old son. The review praises its comic energy and its affection for nightlife without glossing over its messier realities.

image.caption: Miss Benny and Jordan Firstman in Club Kid.

sources.originalTitle: Club Kid review – Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy is irresistible

segments.body: Peter, a Brooklyn club promoter played by Firstman, is forced to rethink his life when a former party acquaintance brings him the son he did not know he had. Their developing relationship gives the film its emotional centre, alongside a lively portrait of New York’s queer club scene.

segments.title: More than a redemption story
segments.body: The review resists reading the film as a simple warning against partying or an argument that parenthood fixes everything. Instead, it finds warmth in a story that acknowledges nightlife’s problems while showing why music, chosen family and shared spaces can matter. Firstman’s humour and the cast’s natural performances are singled out as strengths.

content.headline: James Dean was more than a rebel: the vulnerable actor behind the icon
content.shortHeadline: James Dean beyond the rebel image
content.standfirst: A new adaptation of East of Eden renews attention on Dean, whose career ended at 24. This account looks beyond the familiar image of youthful rebellion to the anxious, emotionally exposed performance that made him endure.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: The article revisits the making of Elia Kazan’s East of Eden, where Dean’s unpredictability unsettled co-star Raymond Massey but helped produce a performance of raw intensity. The film’s most affecting moments, it argues, show a desperate young man rather than the polished rebel of later iconography.

segments.title: A brief career, a lasting image
segments.body: Dean died in a car crash at 24, after only three starring roles. East of Eden was the only one he lived to see released. The account considers how his vulnerable screen presence, including the complicated longing in his performances, became inseparable from a posthumous legend that can overshadow the actor’s work.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility still speaks to the push and pull between heart and head
content.shortHeadline: Sense and Sensibility speaks to the heart-head struggle
content.standfirst: A new adaptation of Jane Austen’s first novel prompts a case for its relevance to a generation balancing emotional openness with caution and insecurity. The film itself, the review says, is darker and less consistent than the celebrated 1995 version.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Georgia Oakley’s adaptation.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility

segments.body: Austen’s sisters Elinor and Marianne respond differently to love and uncertainty: one restrains her feelings, the other invests heavily in romantic hope. The review connects their competing instincts to contemporary pressures around privacy, self-fulfilment and the difficulty of planning for an uncertain future.

segments.title: A new, uneven adaptation
segments.body: Georgia Oakley’s film is described as gloomier than the 1995 adaptation, with Daisy Edgar-Jones praised for conveying Elinor’s contained grief. The review finds the film uneven, but argues that Austen’s story still offers a useful way to think about the risks of suppressing feeling or mistaking romantic optimism for good judgement.

content.headline: Comédie Française turns opening-night chaos into a nimble farce
content.shortHeadline: Comédie Française makes backstage chaos funny
content.standfirst: This French comedy follows a theatre director through the three hours before Macbeth opens, as missing actors, backstage mishaps and a family complication threaten the performance. The review praises the cast’s precision and timing.

image.caption: A scene from Comédie Française.

sources.originalTitle: Comédie Française review – pre-show bedlam plays theatrical chaos for laughs

segments.body: Director Nina arrives without her staff pass and faces a mounting series of crises: a missing Lady Macbeth, unruly performers, technical problems and a visit from the culture minister. The comedy unfolds inside the Paris theatre as opening night approaches.

The review finds the film’s subplot about Nina’s former partner leaving their toddler with her less convincing than its backstage farce. Its strongest appeal is the ensemble’s comic timing and the affectionate picture it draws of theatre people determined to make the show go on.

content.headline: Damilola: The Untold Story remembers a child beyond the crime
content.shortHeadline: Damilola: The Untold Story centres the child and his friends
content.standfirst: John Boyega, his sister and others who knew Damilola Taylor recall the night he was killed and the grief that followed. The documentary focuses on their memories of a friend, rather than turning the case into conventional true crime.

image.caption: Damilola Taylor.

sources.originalTitle: Damilola: The Untold Story review – John Boyega’s trauma after losing his childhood friend is haunting

segments.body: The documentary brings together people who were among the last to see Damilola Taylor alive, including John Boyega, who remembers being frightened by the death of a child. His sister Grace recalls defending Damilola at school and later blaming herself for not walking him home.

segments.title: A community, not a crime scene
segments.body: The film also gives space to memories of North Peckham as a community, rather than reducing the estate to a stereotype. Its stylised recreations and indistinct archival footage avoid forensic spectacle. The review notes that the documentary does not investigate the Preddie brothers’ backgrounds, but says its focus remains with Damilola and those who have carried the loss.

content.headline: Pierre brings a new perspective to British police drama
content.shortHeadline: Pierre brings a fresh perspective to the British cop drama
content.standfirst: David Harewood plays a duty solicitor navigating police cases and institutional racism in a confident Channel 4 noir. The review sees the series as a notable step for Black British crime drama, despite occasional heavy-handed dialogue.

image.caption: David Harewood in Pierre.

sources.originalTitle: Pierre review – David Harewood’s twisty noir is an instant crime classic

segments.body: Pierre is a duty solicitor, not a police officer. When a young Black man who had been building a case of police harassment is found dead, the series draws its crime plot through Pierre’s work and his ties to the community. David Harewood’s performance gives the drama much of its authority.

segments.title: A wider remit than the usual cop show
segments.body: The review argues that Pierre’s position lets the series examine the everyday compromises and indignities of working around the police as a Black professional, while remaining rooted in his community. It praises the confident genre storytelling, though it finds some attempts to compress race and policing debates into dialogue too blunt.

content.headline: The Reluctant Vampire turns Eric Morecambe’s children’s books into comic fun
content.shortHeadline: The Reluctant Vampire is a family comedy with bite
content.standfirst: Lenny Rush leads an ensemble in this gag-filled adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s children’s books. The Guardian praises its warmth, surreal jokes and appeal to adults as well as children.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Valentine in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: The Reluctant Vampire review – Lenny Rush’s absolute joy of a comedy is perfectly cast

segments.body: Valentine is the disappointing second son in a vampire family: he has no fangs, dislikes blood and cannot fly. His mother eventually tells him he is human, rescued as a baby and raised as her own. The discovery sets off a string of misunderstandings and a gently developing friendship.

segments.title: A shared comic sensibility
segments.body: The review praises Lenny Rush and a supporting cast that includes Tom Davis, Sian Clifford, Bill Bailey and Ross Noble. It finds the series faithful to the books’ warmth and daftness while adding jokes for adults, and recommends giving it more than one episode to reach a particularly affectionate Morecambe-inspired gag.

content.headline: Lenny Rush on finding belonging in The Reluctant Vampire
content.shortHeadline: Lenny Rush on belonging and The Reluctant Vampire
content.standfirst: The 17-year-old actor discusses leading a comedy written for him, his admiration for David Brent and the messages he receives from families of disabled children. He sees Valentine’s awkwardness as a familiar story of trying to fit in.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Val in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy

segments.body: Rush says the scripts for The Reluctant Vampire were written with him in mind. He describes the series as a family show that can genuinely work for everyone, and sees its young protagonist’s struggle to belong as relatable beyond the story’s vampires and gargoyles.

segments.title: Visibility and the work
segments.body: Rush says messages from parents whose disabled children have gained confidence from seeing him on screen made him realise the impact of his visibility. He also talks about his ambition to avoid being limited to comedy, his love of The Office, and the importance of his family keeping school and friendships in view alongside acting.

content.headline: Amy Dowden’s early Strictly exit raises questions about the show’s pairings
content.shortHeadline: Amy Dowden’s Strictly exit raises questions about pairings
content.standfirst: The professional dancer has left in the first week for a second consecutive year. The review argues that the show’s pairings shape its emotional appeal and that Dowden deserved a partner with a better chance to show her skill as a teacher and performer.

image.caption: Amy Dowden on Strictly Come Dancing.

sources.originalTitle: Amy Dowden’s exit exposes one big Strictly problem

segments.body: The piece argues that Strictly’s professional dancers, not just its celebrity contestants, are central to the show’s appeal. Their partnerships give viewers a reason to invest, as they help celebrities learn, take risks and change over the series.

segments.title: A difficult run
segments.body: Amy Dowden was paired with celebrity hairdresser Chris Appleton, who left in week one. The writer sets that early exit against Dowden’s recent years on the show, including injury and cancer treatment, and argues that her next series should be defined by her work with a partner rather than by her illness and resilience.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+, has no current Doctor and has cancelled a planned Christmas special. Fans and writers disagree about why the recent run faltered, while holding to the possibility of a return.

image.caption: The Doctors portrayed by Peter Capaldi, Christopher Eccleston, Matt Smith, David Tennant, Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: After the 2025 series starring Ncuti Gatwa, the BBC ended its partnership with Disney+ and put future production out to tender. No company has yet stepped forward, and the BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special. The show currently has no Doctor in place.

segments.title: A changing show, a loyal audience
segments.body: The article traces the series from its 1963 debut through its successful 2005 revival and the more recent change in Doctors and showrunners. Contributors differ over the causes of the latest decline, pointing to scripts, the pace of production and the Disney partnership; fans interviewed remain hopeful that the programme will return.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors makes a spectacular start with Richard E Grant
content.shortHeadline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors slip-up sets the series alight
content.standfirst: Grant accidentally tells Joe Lycett he is a Traitor moments after being chosen, turning a casting reveal into an instant cliffhanger. The review argues that the blunder only heightens the show’s unpredictable appeal.

image.caption: Richard E Grant in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant

segments.body: After being selected alongside Maya Jama as a Traitor, Richard E Grant responds to Joe Lycett’s question by saying, “Oh, I’m a Traitor.” The review confirms it was a genuine mistake, and follows the cast’s confusion as Grant laughs about the slip while Jama considers how they might recover.

segments.title: Why the format still surprises
segments.body: The opening also sets up Ross Kemp’s early suspicions and a cliffhanger in which James Acaster and Amol Rajan must plead for a chance to be recruited. The writer credits the show’s celebrity cast and unpredictable behaviour with renewing the pleasures of a familiar reality-game format.

content.headline: The final 70 Up asks what its participants think of the experiment
content.shortHeadline: 70 Up ends by questioning its own legacy
content.standfirst: As the long-running documentary series concludes, its participants revisit not only their lives but the way they were represented. The final episodes include criticism of director Michael Apted and the limitations of reducing decades of experience to a few hours of television.

image.caption: Participants in the 7 Up documentary series as children.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A little pill of poison’: Why the cast of 70 Up came to resent it

segments.body: 70 Up brings the series that began in 1964 as Seven Up! to a close. The programme follows the surviving participants and reflects on lives shaped by circumstance, opportunity and change. Producer Helen Houston says the series has reached a natural endpoint.

segments.title: The people behind the portrait
segments.body: The finale also returns to participants’ dissatisfaction with how they were portrayed. Peter Davies describes leaving after a tabloid backlash; John Brisby says he disliked being cast as a token toff, and earlier footage shows Jackie Basset challenging Apted’s treatment of women. The series remains compelling, the review argues, but its subjects know that the edit can never contain a whole life.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has excellent combat but little else to sustain it
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day’s combat can’t save its repetition
content.standfirst: The prequel recreates the alien invasion that shaped the series, and its cover-based shooting feels better than ever. But the review finds repetitive levels, intrusive collectibles and too few ideas beyond the firefights.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day places Marcus Fenix and his squad at the start of the Locust invasion. The opening delivers the series’ familiar mix of destruction, tactical cover and chainsaw combat, and the review calls the movement and firefights the best the games have offered.

segments.title: A strong core stretched thin
segments.body: The praise is undercut by levels that repeatedly send players across the same spaces, large areas crowded with collectibles and side objectives, and moments when exploration can trigger a mission failure. The reviewer finds that the game’s strongest ideas arrive early, leaving its excellent combat surrounded by repetition.

content.headline: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil recreates the feeling of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil captures the unease of playing the game
content.standfirst: The adaptation leaves familiar heroes aside to follow an ordinary courier through escalating danger, scarce ammunition and recognisable locations. The argument is that its fidelity lies in recreating the games’ structure and vulnerability, not simply their characters.

image.caption: Zach Cregger and Austin Abrams on the set of the Resident Evil film.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: The film follows courier Bryan Hodukavich as a virus outbreak engulfs Raccoon City. He starts without weapons or a clear understanding of events, then finds equipment while moving through an abandoned farmhouse, tunnel, hospital and sewer. Typewriters and fragments of recorded information echo the games’ conventions.

segments.title: A film shaped like a game
segments.body: The writer argues that Cregger’s approach reproduces the player’s uncertain progress through an unfamiliar world, rather than following familiar characters such as Leon or Claire. Its vulnerable protagonist recalls the series creator’s view that horror is strongest when survival never feels assured.

content.headline: How to protect children from Roblox phishing scams
content.shortHeadline: Roblox phishing scams target children’s accounts and Robux
content.standfirst: Fraudsters lure players to convincing fake login pages with promises of free in-game currency. Security experts advise opening Roblox directly and treating authentication codes like passwords.

image.caption: Roblox users are advised to use the official app or website and avoid unknown links.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.body: Scammers promise free Robux through links shared in YouTube or TikTok comments and Discord chats. The links lead to lookalike Roblox sign-in pages that collect usernames, passwords and sometimes two-factor codes before redirecting the child to the real site.

segments.title: Steps to reduce the risk
segments.body: NordVPN researchers say they found almost 200 addresses offering ready-made phishing pages during a seven-day period. The practical advice is to open Roblox through its official app or website rather than links, and never share authentication or backup codes. Roblox says it cannot guarantee it will restore lost currency or items.

content.headline: A father and son revisit the Call of Duty missions they first played together
content.shortHeadline: Replaying Call of Duty brings a father and son together
content.standfirst: Nearly two decades after playing Modern Warfare 2 together when his son was five, the writer returns to its co-op missions with him as an adult. The game becomes a way to rediscover teamwork, shared memories and time together.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game revisited by a father and son.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The pair return to missions they never completed the first time around. Their approaches still differ: the father advances cautiously, while his son charges ahead. They eventually learn to compromise, taking out the game’s notorious guard dogs first and completing a mission that has eluded them for 17 years.

segments.title: Play as a shared memory
segments.body: As they move through more missions, the writer reflects on the rare pleasure of playing without the pressure to make time productive. Their time in the flat is temporary, with the pair soon moving to different parts of the world, but his son tells him he will remember it as some of their best times together.

content.headline: The volunteer Pokémon professors who keep competitive play running
content.shortHeadline: Meet the volunteers behind Pokémon’s competitive tournaments
content.standfirst: At the 2026 world championships, volunteer professors served as judges, teachers and event staff. Their work ranges from checking results and explaining rules to helping players feel welcome and keeping the venue safe.

image.caption: Attendees at the 2026 Pokémon World Championships in San Francisco.

sources.originalTitle: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling

segments.body: The Pokémon Professor Program is a global network of volunteers who help run official events. Around 300 professors attended the 2026 world championships in San Francisco, taking on roles that included refereeing card games, supporting players and managing event logistics.

segments.title: Rules, care and difficult calls
segments.body: Head judge Gemma Byard describes the work of checking match results, maintaining safety and handling disputes. Evelyne de Groot compares the role to customer service: professors must know the game and give clear guidance so players can enjoy competing. The Pokémon Company International declined to provide an official explanation of how professors are compensated.

content.headline: Why some players see GTA VI’s in-game romance as a relationship issue
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s romance debate taps real relationship worries
content.standfirst: Online arguments over whether playing a romance with Lucia or Jason counts as cheating have focused on the game’s relationship mechanics. The article suggests the controversy also reflects real concerns about attention, loneliness and unmet needs.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: The game’s protagonists, Lucia and Jason, can strengthen their bond through interactions including dates, messages and time together. Some social-media users say engaging with those features crosses a relationship boundary; others dismiss the objection as jealousy.

segments.title: Virtual romance, real boundaries
segments.body: The writer argues that the reaction may point to genuine concerns about partners feeling overlooked, particularly in a broader climate of loneliness and disconnection. They do not consider in-game romance cheating, while acknowledging that couples can set different boundaries and that AI companionship raises a separate question.

content.headline: The White House’s pixel-art games use play to push anti-migrant messaging
content.shortHeadline: White House arcade turns games into anti-migrant propaganda
content.standfirst: A set of games on the US government’s website borrows familiar formats to promote hostile messages about migrants and other targets. The article argues that the project shows how political rhetoric can appropriate gaming aesthetics and participation.

image.caption: Build the Wall, one of the games in the White House arcade.

sources.originalTitle: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade

segments.body: The arcade includes a Tetris-like game called Build the Wall and a Snake-style game in which players collect migrants along the Rio Grande. The writer describes the games as mean-spirited and crude, with a cutesy pixel-art style that makes their dehumanising premise no less explicit.

segments.title: From imagery to interaction
segments.body: Games have long been used to explore political subjects, the article notes, but this is a government deploying playable material as part of its messaging. Author George Osborn sees the arcade as an escalation from appropriating gaming culture on social media to using games themselves to reach audiences.

content.headline: Physics Nobel honours Francis Halzen and IceCube’s neutrino discoveries
content.shortHeadline: Francis Halzen wins Nobel for IceCube neutrino work
content.standfirst: The physicist helped turn a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into a detector for high-energy particles from space. The work opened a new way to study the cosmos, beyond light and gravitational waves.

image.caption: The IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station in Antarctica.

sources.originalTitle: Nobel prize in physics goes to Francis Halzen for south pole work on neutrinos

segments.body: Francis Halzen, a Belgian particle physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, has won the 2026 Nobel prize in physics for decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. IceCube detected its first high-energy neutrinos from beyond Earth in 2013.

segments.title: A new way to observe the universe
segments.body: IceCube uses thousands of light sensors embedded in a cubic kilometre of clear Antarctic ice to detect faint flashes caused when neutrinos collide with atomic nuclei. The particles pass through matter readily; detecting them gives researchers another way to investigate distant and extreme cosmic phenomena.

content.headline: Cancer diagnoses are rising among under-50s in three countries
content.shortHeadline: Study finds rising rates of seven early-onset cancers in England
content.standfirst: A World Cancer Research Fund analysis found significant increases in several cancer types among younger adults in England, the US and the Netherlands. The causes are not fully understood, and earlier detection may explain only part of the trend.

image.caption: A patient receives a CT scan. Earlier detection may account for part of the rise in cancer diagnoses.

sources.originalTitle: Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds

segments.body: Analysis of cancer data from England, the US and the Netherlands found rising rates of several cancers diagnosed before age 50. In England, prostate cancer incidence in men under 50 rose from 1 per 100,000 in 2001 to 3.6 in 2023; bowel cancer rates among under-50s more than doubled, from 3.9 to 8.4 per 100,000.

segments.title: Why the pattern is not yet explained
segments.body: Researchers and the World Cancer Research Fund point to possible contributions from obesity, diet, exercise, alcohol, smoking and environmental exposures, alongside greater awareness and earlier diagnosis. The researchers say increased diagnosis does not account for the whole rise, and further research is needed. Cancer remains much more common in older adults.

content.headline: Medicine Nobel recognises discoveries behind optogenetics
content.shortHeadline: Nobel honours the discoveries that made optogenetics possible
content.standfirst: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel share the 2026 medicine prize for work on light-gated ion channels. The technique lets researchers use light to control nerve cells and investigate how brain circuits function.

image.caption: The three Nobel medicine laureates appear on a screen during the prize announcement.

sources.originalTitle: Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

segments.body: The Nobel prize in physiology or medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. Their research helped establish a way to switch nerve cells on or off using light, giving scientists a tool to investigate neural circuits in living brains.

segments.title: From algae to brain research
segments.body: Hegemann studied how green algae respond to light, while Hegemann and Nagel identified channelrhodopsins—proteins that allow charged particles to flow through cells when exposed to light. Deisseroth and colleagues later used the approach to trigger activity in nerve cells in mice and study circuits involved in movement and memory.

segments.title: Early therapeutic work
segments.body: The reporting describes optogenetic therapy as a developing field. In one trial, the technique was used to partially restore sight in a man with retinitis pigmentosa, using a harmless virus to deliver genetic instructions to retinal cells and goggles to stimulate them with light. That result does not establish a general treatment for brain disorders.

content.headline: Global study finds women report more pain than men across the body
content.shortHeadline: Women report more pain across 11 body sites, global study finds
content.standfirst: Researchers analysed self-reported pain data from more than six million people in 118 countries. They found higher reported pain among women at every body site studied, while noting limits in regional coverage and measurement.

image.caption: The study found women reported more pain than men at all 11 bodily sites examined.

sources.originalTitle: Women suffer more pain than men across the whole body, major global study finds

segments.body: A study drawing on data from more than six million people aged five to over 100 found women reported more pain than men across all 11 bodily sites examined, with particularly high differences for headache, facial and abdominal pain. The data covered 118 countries between 1990 and 2025.

segments.title: Pain across a lifetime
segments.body: For both sexes, the steepest rise in reported pain occurred before 55, while high-intensity pain peaked around 50. Back, hip and knee pain generally increased with age. The authors say the results can help guide prevention and care, but the study describes patterns in age groups rather than following the same people over time.

segments.title: Limits and implications
segments.body: The researchers used self-reported pain partly because estimates based on diagnoses may miss people with limited healthcare access. They also note uneven coverage across regions and age groups and differences in how pain was measured. Commenting on the findings, experts called for women’s pain to be taken seriously and for research and care to address the gender gap.

content.headline: Climate change is prompting researchers to test new crops for Britain
content.shortHeadline: Hotter, drier summers prompt a search for new UK crops
content.standfirst: Researchers are testing drought-tolerant crops such as lupins and chickpeas as heat and dry weather affect British harvests. Which varieties can thrive—and where—still needs investigation.

image.caption: A lupin bhaji made with flour from a crop researchers are testing for future food production.
